holding_summary: The Court of Appeals held that General Hancock and his family, though occupying hotel rooms under an understanding as to price and expected length of stay, remained transient guests rather than boarders because no binding contract fixed a definite term and Hancock, as an army officer with no permanent home, could be ordered away at any moment. Because the hotel failed to post the statutory notice limiting innkeeper liability, it was held liable as insurer for property stolen from the plaintiff's rooms. The court distinguished this case from ones where an explicit boarding contract had stripped the occupant of a guest's protections.

quotes.text: Officers of the army and navy, and soldiers and sailors, who have no permanent residence which they can call home, may well be regarded as travelers or wayfarers when stopping at public inns or hotels, and to make them chargeable as mere boarders it should be shown satisfactorily that an explicit contract had been made which deprived them of the privileges and rights which their vocation conferred upon them as passengers or travelers.

The common-law rule which fixes the liability of an innkeeper to his guest is a salutary one and imposes no needless hardship upon him, and it should be administered according to its spirit without regard to technical distinctions.
but he may, by a special contract to board and sojourn, make himself a boarder, and being such the innkeeper is not liable.
we think the defendants are bound within the reason of the rule under which an innkeeper is held liable for the goods and property of his guest.

notes: Not a householder-letting case; concerns the guest-vs-boarder distinction for innkeeper liability at a commercial hotel. Marked mixed: broadly protects transient lodgers' rights while reaffirming that an explicit boarding contract strips those protections.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: The court held that a restrictive covenant barring certain business uses did not prohibit operating a private hotel or boarding house on the restricted property, because the practical construction the parties had given the covenant -- years of unobjected-to private hotels and boarding houses on other restricted parcels -- showed such use was not meant to be barred. The defendant's establishment, though larger and more elaborately furnished than its neighbors, was a private boarding house rather than an ordinary inn because it did not bid indiscriminately for transient travelers, so it fell outside the covenant's prohibition.

quotes.text: An inn or hotel proper is conducted for the purpose of entertaining travelers and all respectable persons who apply for accommodation. It bids indiscriminately for the patronage of transient and permanent guests. The Victoria did not entertain travelers as such.

I therefore decide that the Victoria is a private hotel or boarding house of the same general character as the other hotels or boarding houses named, and therefore not within the prohibition of the covenant.

for many years there have been erected and continuously conducted upon parcels of the restricted property private hotels or boarding houses without remonstrance, and without suggestion from any one that the covenant was thereby violated.
